Arrays can serve as the implicit storage substrate for binary heaps and complete binary trees: binary heaps use 2i+1/2i+2 indexing (0-based) to eliminate pointer overhead, and complete binary trees use the same index formulas for parent-child navigation. Both exploit O(1) array access, with the address formula B + c·i as a underlying mechanism for element location.

### array-layout-governs-cache-performance [IN] DERIVED
Array memory layout (row-major C convention vs column-major Fortran convention) determines which iteration patterns achieve the optimal ⌈nk/B⌉ cache miss rate: iterating along the contiguous storage dimension exploits spatial locality, while cross-dimension iteration degrades to one useful element per cache line fetch — making layout choice a first-order performance decision.

### astar-consistent-equiv-dijkstra [IN] OBSERVATION
With a consistent heuristic, A* is equivalent to running Dijkstra's algorithm with reduced edge costs d'(x,y) = d(x,y) + h(y) - h(x)

### astar-consistent-heuristic [IN] OBSERVATION
A consistent (monotone) heuristic satisfies h(x) <= d(x,y) + h(y) for every edge (x,y); consistency implies admissibility but not vice versa; with consistency, no node is expanded more than once
- Source: wiki:A*_search_algorithm

### astar-dijkstra-special-case [IN] OBSERVATION

### avl-balance-factor [IN] OBSERVATION
Balance factor BF(X) = Height(RightSubtree(X)) - Height(LeftSubtree(X)). Only 2 bits per node needed to store it. BF < 0 is left-heavy, BF > 0 is right-heavy, BF = 0 is balanced.
- Source: wiki:AVL_tree

### avl-complexity [IN] OBSERVATION
AVL tree operations: Search O(log n), Insert O(log n), Delete O(log n) -- all worst-case. Space O(n). These bounds hold for both amortized and worst case.
- Source: wiki:AVL_tree

### avl-definition [IN] OBSERVATION
An AVL tree is a self-balancing binary search tree where the balance factor (height difference of child subtrees) of every node is in {-1, 0, +1}. Named after Adelson-Velsky and Landis (1962), it was the first self-balancing BST.
- Source: wiki:AVL_tree

### avl-delete-may-cascade [IN] DERIVED
AVL deletion may require O(log n) rotations because a rotation during delete can decrease the subtree height, propagating imbalance upward (unlike insert where rotation restores height)
- Source: wiki:AVL_tree
- Depends on: avl-rotations, avl-insert-retrace

### avl-insert-max-one-rotation [IN] DERIVED
AVL insertion requires at most one rotation (single or double) to rebalance because insertion increases subtree height by at most 1, and a single rotation restores the original height
- Source: wiki:AVL_tree
- Depends on: avl-rotations, avl-insert-retrace

### avl-insert-retrace [IN] OBSERVATION
AVL insert retracing: BF becomes 0 -> stop (height unchanged). BF becomes +/-1 -> continue (height increased). BF becomes +/-2 -> rotate then stop (height restored). Retracing is O(1) amortized.
- Source: wiki:AVL_tree

### avl-join-split [IN] OBSERVATION
AVL trees support Join and Split operations enabling efficient set operations (union, intersection, difference) in O(m log(n/m + 1)) time. Join requires at most 2 rotations. Split costs O(log n). These operations are parallelizable with depth O(log m * log n).

### tree-dual-encoding-strategies [OUT] DERIVED
Trees admit two fundamentally different encoding strategies that trade flexibility for efficiency: array-implicit encoding (heaps, Fenwick) eliminates pointers via arithmetic but restricts to specific tree shapes, while structural encoding (red-black as binary 2-3-4 trees) translates multi-way invariants into binary constraints, preserving structural flexibility at the cost of per-node metadata.

### union-find-amortized-coevolution [OUT] DERIVED
Union-find exemplifies the coevolution of data structure design and analysis technique: its orthogonal optimization axes (path compression variants for find, rank/size heuristics for union) produce the near-constant alpha(n) amortized bound that makes Kruskal's algorithm edge-sort-dominated — and amortized analysis was the analytical framework (formalized by Tarjan in 1985) that made this bound expressible in the first place.

### union-find-definition [OUT] OBSERVATION
A disjoint-set (union-find) data structure maintains a collection of disjoint sets with three operations: MakeSet (create singleton set), Find (determine which set an element belongs to), and Union (merge two sets), represented as a forest of rooted trees
- Source: entries/2026/06/19/wiki-Disjoint-set_data_structure.md

### union-find-history [OUT] OBSERVATION
Union-find was invented by Galler and Fischer in 1964; Tarjan proved the O(m·α(n)) upper bound in 1975; Fredman and Saks proved the matching Ω(m·α(n)) lower bound in 1989

### union-find-kruskal [OUT] OBSERVATION
Union-find is used in Kruskal's minimum spanning tree algorithm to efficiently detect whether adding an edge would create a cycle, by checking if both endpoints are in the same set

### union-find-union-strategies [OUT] OBSERVATION
Union by rank attaches the shorter tree under the root of the taller tree; union by size attaches the tree with fewer nodes under the root of the larger tree. Both strategies guarantee O(log n) tree height without path compression.
